checks.demonstration: Consider one required update with \(f=\tanh\), pretrained scalar weights \(1\) and \(1+\varepsilon\), fixed \(1/2<\alpha<1\), and input uniform on \(\{-2,-1,1,2\}\). Set all weight perturbations to zero. The needed correction is \[F(x)=(1-\alpha)\{\tanh((1+\varepsilon)x)-\tanh x\}.\] In the appendix’s fixed-routing construction, every mixture of scalar linear controls is \(cx\). For \(x>0\), \(F(x)/x=(1-\alpha)\int_1^{1+\varepsilon}\operatorname{sech}^2(tx)\,dt\), which strictly decreases with \(x\) when \(\varepsilon>0\). Thus \(F(2)\ne2F(1)\), and the exact least-squares residual is \[\min_c\mathbb E(F(X)-cX)^2=\frac{(2F(1)-F(2))^2}{10}>0.\] This persists as \(\xi\to0\). The mismatch can therefore occur with arbitrarily small fixed mixing constants.

A vanishing-error theorem needs that distance, the mixing residuals and the Taylor terms to vanish together; \(\xi\to0\) alone is insufficient. A precise alternative is to keep unrestricted function-valued controls: for a fixed routing map \(h_t\), let \(P\) send the control vector to \((g_{h_t})_t\). checks.location: Proposition 4.4 (Sec. 4.3), the two sentences after Eq. (12); compare the assumptions of Proposition 4.2 and Appendix A.4
checks.claim: Under Proposition 4.2's assumptions one additionally gets epsK^2 < epsc^2, hence eps^2 < epsc^2: routing is said to strictly reduce the representation error relative to block-local Parallel Control.
checks.explanation: A smaller routed control norm can move an already optimal local control away from the task target. The blockwise implication therefore needs a comparison of approximation errors. Requiring strictly smaller routed norm bounds at every site of the shared finite expert pool instead makes the premise impossible at a minimum-bound site; it does not provide a useful strict-improvement result.
checks.demonstration:
Let $e_1=(1,0)^\top$, let the input at the block under consideration be $x=e_1$, and take two rank-at-most-one experts

$$\Delta W_1=e_1e_1^\top=B_1A_1,\qquad \Delta W_2=0=B_2A_2,$$

where $B_1=e_1$, $B_2=0$, and $A_1=A_2=e_1^\top$. Thus the factor bounds hold with $\beta_1=1$, $\beta_2=0$, and $\gamma=1$. Choose zero frozen dynamics and a top-one router that selects expert 2 at $x$; two gate logits $0$ and $1$ realize this selection, and the selected weight is normalized to one. Both comparison paths start at $e_1$. The conditional routed magnitude is then $\mathbb E[\beta_K(x)\mid x]=0<\beta_1$ at block 1.

Take the task-optimal control to be $\Delta W^*=e_1e_1^\top$. This can be realized by a squared-error target whose desired next state is $2e_1$. The local control is exactly optimal, whereas the routed control is zero. With $\alpha=3/4$,

$$\bar\epsilon_c^2=0,\qquad \bar\epsilon_K^2=1,\qquad \bar\epsilon^2=\left\|\frac34e_1-e_1\right\|^2=\frac1{16}.$$

Every norm and factorization premise used in the one-step comparison holds at this block, yet routing increases the approximation error. The valid convex upper bound gives $1/16\le1/4$. A norm controls distance from zero, whereas representation error measures distance from the task-optimal control; these are different comparisons.

The quantifier over blocks matters. If the strict condition in Proposition 4.2 is required simultaneously at every site in the same finite expert pool, it cannot hold. At a site $t_*$ with $\beta_{t_*}=\min_k\beta_k$, every convex routed average satisfies $\beta_K(x)\ge\beta_{t_*}$, and so does its conditional expectation. The example above is therefore a counterexample to the meaningful blockwise norm-to-error inference, not a network satisfying a globally impossible strict premise. The latter reading makes the claimed consequence vacuous; it does not establish a useful representation-improvement theorem.

Appendix A.4 proves only the convex error bound, ending at its Equation (39). It introduces no alignment assumption or comparison between routed and local approximation errors. The same strict-improvement sentence is present in both public versions. This establishes a missing condition for the representation-improvement interpretation, without contradicting Equation (12), the mixing architecture, or the reported experiments.
checks.repair:
Keep Equation (12) and make strict improvement conditional on approximation error, not on operator norm alone. For fixed $x$, define the local residual $c=\Delta W_tx-\Delta W^*x$ and routed residual $r=\sum_k\pi_k(x)\Delta W_kx-\Delta W^*x$. Assume finite second moments and normalized nonnegative routing weights. With a fixed $\alpha\in[0,1]$, the exact identity is

$$\mathbb E[\|\alpha c+(1-\alpha)r\|^2\mid x]
=\alpha\mathbb E[\|c\|^2\mid x]+(1-\alpha)\mathbb E[\|r\|^2\mid x]
-\alpha(1-\alpha)\mathbb E[\|c-r\|^2\mid x].$$

It follows by expanding the squared norm and collecting the cross term; dropping the last, nonpositive term proves Equation (12). If $\alpha<1$ and $\mathbb E[\|r\|^2\mid x]<\mathbb E[\|c\|^2\mid x]$, the right side is strictly below the local error. At $\alpha=1$ the mixture equals the local control, so strict improvement is impossible. The same proof holds for averages over a common distribution of inputs and sites when the strict error comparison is imposed on those averages.

These are sufficient conditions for the stated representation benefit. Proposition 4.2's norm comparison does not imply them. The corrected statement must therefore either add this error comparison as an assumption or retain only the convex bound and remove the asserted automatic strict benefit. Any norm condition used across depth must also specify the sites where it is assumed, because a strict reduction in the routed norm bound at every site in one finite expert pool is impossible at a minimum-bound site.

Appendix B.1 specifies $w^*\sim\mathcal N(0,I_{20})$ once per trial, independent features $x_1,x_2\sim\mathcal N(0,I_{20})$, and labels

$$Y=\mathbf1\{D+\epsilon>0\},\qquad D=(w^*)^\top(x_1-x_2),\qquad \epsilon\sim\mathcal N(0,0.5^2).$$

It then describes roughly 30% of pairs as ambiguous and says that a noisy label can differ from its noiseless counterpart. The previous calculation concerns a well-defined but different quantity. Conditional on $w^*\ne0$, write $R=\|w^*\|$ and $s=\sqrt2R$. Then $D=sZ$ and $\epsilon=0.5T$ for independent standard normals $Z,T$. The rotationally symmetric vector $(Z,T)$ has uniform angle. $$q(w^*)=\Pr\!\left(Y\ne\mathbf1\{D>0\}\mid w^*\right)

checks.claim: Symmetric label-flip corruption makes teacher unbiased.
checks.explanation: No issue was found in the checked claims. The passage explicitly identifies class symmetry as its local meaning and does not use that symmetry to set $B(\theta)=0$. Symmetric flips can change the expected Bradley–Terry gradient, but this fact does not contradict the described sampling mechanism or a later inference made from it.
checks.demonstration:
Let $X$ denote a preference pair, $Y\in\{0,1\}$ its clean label, and $\widetilde Y$ the label obtained by independently flipping $Y$ with probability $\rho\in(0,1/2)$. Write $\eta(x)=\Pr(Y=1\mid X=x)$. Symmetric corruption gives

$$\mathbb E[\widetilde Y\mid X=x]=\rho+(1-2\rho)\eta(x).$$

This differs from $\eta(x)$ unless $\eta(x)=1/2$ or $\rho=0$. Nevertheless,

$$\Pr(\widetilde Y=1\mid X=x)-\frac12=(1-2\rho)\left(\eta(x)-\frac12\right),$$

so the Bayes binary decision boundary is unchanged. With balanced labels, even the marginal means can agree: $\mathbb E Y=1/2$ implies $\mathbb E\widetilde Y=1/2$. These facts support the paper's intended distinction between class-symmetric corruption and errors concentrated on particular response styles. They do not imply zero gradient bias.

For the Bradley–Terry loss, let $m_\theta(X)$ be the model's reward difference, $J_\theta(X)=\nabla_\theta m_\theta(X)$, and $s(u)=1/(1+e^{-u})$. Its gradient is $(s(m_\theta(X))-Y)J_\theta(X)$. Taking expectations over the flip gives the population gradient difference

$$B(\theta)=\mathbb E[\nabla_\theta\ell(\theta;X,\widetilde Y)-\nabla_\theta\ell(\theta;X,Y)]
=\rho\,\mathbb E[(2Y-1)J_\theta(X)].$$

This is the teacher-gradient bias $\nabla\mathcal L^f-\nabla\mathcal L$ used in the paper's theory. Class symmetry does not force the vector expectation to vanish.

For a balanced example, take a scalar frozen feature difference $Z\in\{-1,1\}$ with equal probabilities, reward margin $m_\theta=\theta Z$, and conditional label probabilities $\Pr(Y=1\mid Z=1)=3/4$ and $\Pr(Y=1\mid Z=-1)=1/4$. The model is correctly specified at $\theta_* =\log 3$. Its clean expected gradient is zero, its label marginal is exactly balanced, and the corrupted label marginal remains balanced. Yet $\mathbb E[(2Y-1)Z]=1/2$, so the corrupted expected gradient at $\theta_*$ equals $\rho/2>0$. The example uses precisely a trainable scalar score head on fixed features and symmetric flips.

Section 5.2 immediately explains its word unbiased by class-symmetric noise and contrasts it with structural bias. It does not set $B(\theta)=0$ in a subsequent bound or calculation; the ABC estimator is designed to accommodate nonzero teacher bias. Thus the source already identifies the operative meaning of the description. The example distinguishes that meaning from gradient unbiasedness; it does not refute the stated sampling mechanism or an inference that the manuscript makes. The immediate contextual explanation identifies class symmetry, so the stronger gradient-unbiasedness interpretation is not a premise of the stated experiment.

checks.location: Appendix B.4, proof of Thm 2.5, step from Cor 2.3 to Eq. (11); Theorem 2.5 statement
checks.claim: At the optimum (G*,D*), for any incomplete observation with mask m0, averaging D*'s normalised output over G*'s imputations gives P(Y=i|x_obs) (Thm 2.5), via Eq. (11) X_hat*_miss|x_obs =d X_miss|x_obs.
checks.explanation: Several mask-specific completed-data laws can average to the correct marginal while each remains incorrect. Preserving observed coordinates does not identify the missing conditional distribution from this mixture. The proof requires alignment conditional on the mask, which the stated objective does not enforce.
checks.demonstration:
Partition $[0,1]^2$ into four half-square cells, indexed by $A=\mathbf1\{X_1\ge1/2\}$ and $B=\mathbf1\{X_2\ge1/2\}$. Use uniform density within each cell and cell masses
$$P=\begin{pmatrix}.2&.3\\.2&.3\end{pmatrix}.$$
Let $\Pr(Y=1\mid X)=.1+.8B$. Give complete cases probability $1/2$ and each of the two one-coordinate-observed masks probability $1/4$, independently of $(X,Y)$. This is MCAR.

A generator can preserve the observed coordinate and produce cell-mass matrices
$$Q_A=\begin{pmatrix}.35&.15\\.05&.45\end{pmatrix},\qquad Q_B=\begin{pmatrix}.05&.45\\.35&.15\end{pmatrix}.$$
The row sums of $Q_A$ and column sums of $Q_B$ match those of $P$, and $(Q_A+Q_B)/2=P$. Sampling the missing coordinate uniformly within its chosen half therefore attains exact pooled alignment with genuine continuous densities.

For the mask observing $X_1$, at any $x_1<1/2$ the imputer gives $\Pr(B=1)=.3$ instead of $.6$. The averaged normalized discriminator output is $.1+.8(.3)=.34$, whereas the true posterior is $.1+.8(.6)=.58$. All class probabilities are strictly positive, so the optimal discriminator is attained in its stated interior domain. The resulting label is wrong: its conditional error is $.58$ instead of the Bayes error $.42$.
checks.repair:
Require or enforce alignment separately for every mask of positive probability:
$$\mathcal L(\widehat X\mid M=m)=\mathcal L(X\mid M=m).$$
Together with observed-coordinate preservation and MCAR, this identifies the required missing-feature conditional law. Averaging the complete-data posterior over that law then gives the Bayes posterior by the tower property. A mask-conditioned alignment objective is one possible way to supply the missing requirement. Pooled alignment alone is insufficient.
checks.scope: The example satisfies the pooled alignment condition and the complete-case discriminator identity used by the proof. It refutes the maskwise conclusion for a general optimal generator. Restricting to a single incomplete mask or establishing maskwise alignment would remove this particular obstruction.
checks.claimFormula: \mathcal L(\widehat X)=\mathcal L(X)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\mathcal L(\widehat X_{\rm miss}\mid x_{\rm obs},M=m)=\mathcal L(X_{\rm miss}\mid x_{\rm obs})
checks.claimContext: The discriminator observes a completed feature vector and a complete-versus-incomplete class. The generator additionally receives the detailed missingness mask. Theorem 2.5 uses pooled distribution alignment to claim Bayes-optimal prediction for every fixed incomplete mask under MCAR.
checks.title: Pooled imputation alignment does not identify each mask-specific posterior
checks.whyItMatters: The central theoretical guarantee concerns prediction for a particular partially observed patient or example. Correct aggregate imputation statistics do not ensure correct predictions for each observation pattern.

checks.location: Appendix A.2, Lemma A.5, lines 1514-1567; arbitrary-r high-probability tail l2 bound
checks.claim: For every integer cutoff r, the displayed tail-frequency l2 estimate holds with probability 1-O(d^-M), where M can be any sufficiently large constant.
checks.explanation: When the expected number of tail observations tends to zero, a single observation still has polynomial probability. On that event the empirical norm is much larger than the displayed bound.
checks.demonstration:
Choose $\alpha=2$, $N=d^7$, $p_i=i^{-2}/H_{N,2}$, batch size $B=1$ and cutoff $r=d$. On the event that the single draw lies beyond $d$, the tail norm is exactly one.

Because $H_{N,2}\leq2$, the $d$ indices $d+1,\ldots,2d$ alone have probability at least $1/(8d)$. Yet the asserted right side is $C\log d/\sqrt d\to0$ for every fixed implicit constant $C$. Failure is therefore at least $1/(8d)$ for large $d$, rather than $O(d^{-M})$ for $M>1$. Gaussian embeddings place no further restriction on this sampling example.
checks.repair:
Retain the rare-count term. Let $\rho_r=\sum_{i>r}p_i$. Under the paper's $N=\operatorname{poly}(d)$ convention, take $L$ to be a sufficiently large multiple of $\log d$ for the desired polynomial confidence; more generally, take $L\geq\log((N+1)/\eta)$ for failure probability $\eta$. Binomial concentration and a union bound give
$$N_{>r}/B\lesssim\rho_r+L/B,\qquad
\|q_{>r}\|_\infty\lesssim r^{-\alpha}+L/B.$$
Since $\|q_{>r}\|_2^2\leq\|q_{>r}\|_\infty N_{>r}/B$, a valid replacement is
$$\|q_{>r}\|_2^2\lesssim(r^{-\alpha}+L/B)(r^{1-\alpha}+L/B).$$
This also supplies the frequency event used at $r\asymp d/(\log d)^2$. Writing $A=\max\{r^{-\alpha}\log d,(\log d)/B\}$, the two factors are at most constant multiples of $A$ and $(r/\log d+1)A$. Hence $\|q_{>r}\|_2/\sqrt d\lesssim A$, as required there. The dense-tail estimate may be stated separately.
checks.scope: The arbitrary-cutoff high-confidence estimate is false. The additive correction is sufficient for the specified frequency-event use; this counterexample does not establish failure of a main recovery exponent.
checks.claimContext: Lemma A.5 gives an empirical tail-frequency bound for every integer cutoff, with failure probability $O(d^{-M})$ for any sufficiently large fixed $M$. Its sparse-tail proof treats a binomial count as comparable to its mean.
checks.title: A rare tail observation invalidates the all-cutoff confidence bound

checks.demonstration:
Take \(r=N=L=1\), \(K=2\) and \(M=1\), with any fixed positive \(C_3\). For each arm there is at most one agent block, two assortment blocks (including the empty assortment), and one agent–assortment block. Every allocation is at most \(\lceil T_1\rceil\), because the design weights are probabilities. Thus the first epoch has at most
\[8\lceil C_3\log T\log^2(2T)\rceil=O(\log^3T)<T\]
rounds for sufficiently large \(T\). Elimination can only shorten it. If the specified designs are well-defined and the algorithm continues to the horizon, it must start a second epoch, contradicting \(\tau_T\le1\). \[T_\tau=\eta_T^{2(1-2^{-\tau})},\qquad rKT_M=T.\]
Hence the horizon ends no later than epoch \(M\). The logit Jacobian gives a positive-definite metric \(G=J^\top(\operatorname{diag}p-pp^\top)J\). Under \(s=2\sqrt p\), this is the induced metric of the radius-two sphere, with Gaussian curvature \(1/4\). The Euclidean metric on the same coordinate domain has curvature zero. Curvature depends on metric derivatives, not merely its pointwise matrix congruence. The background justification fails; no numerical fit depends on this equality. The weaker intrinsic-dimension statement need not change.
